chapters.title: Chapter 5: Applying Duration and Convexity as an Indian Investor

lessons.title: Duration Through RBI Rate Cycles: Gilt Fund Returns from 2019 to 2024

children.text: Four chapters of formulas come down to one practical question: what actually happens to your money when RBI changes course? India ran a full rate cycle between 2019 and 2024. Yields fell hard into the pandemic, stayed low for two years, rose sharply through 2022, and drifted back down. A long duration gilt fund and a short duration fund lived through exactly the same six years and the same policy decisions, and their investors had completely different experiences. This lesson walks through that cycle year by year and shows you where duration helped and where it hurt.

body.text: Duration does not make a fund better or worse. It decides how much of your return comes from steady income and how much from the price swings of a rate cycle you cannot forecast.

Important: the fund returns in this lesson are modelled, not actual scheme returns. They are built by applying the duration and convexity maths from Chapters 3 and 4 to approximate calendar-year moves in the 10-year G-Sec yield, for two illustrative funds. Real schemes change duration over time, hold bonds other than the 10-year benchmark, and report their own audited returns. Use the pattern here to understand cause and effect, not as a record of what any fund delivered.

children.text: Start with what RBI did and roughly where the 10-year G-Sec yield ended each year. The yield levels below are approximate, rounded to give the shape of the cycle rather than exact closing prints.

body.caption: The 2019 to 2024 rate cycle (repo rate actual, 10-year G-Sec yields approximate)

cells: Pandemic cuts to 4.00%, heavy liquidity support
On hold at 4.00% as inflation builds
Hikes begin in May, repo reaches 6.25%
One final hike to 6.50% in February, then a long pause

body.text: Notice how loosely the repo rate and the 10-year yield are connected. In 2021 the repo did not move at all, yet the 10-year yield rose 55 basis points as the market began pricing in future hikes. In 2024 the repo again did not move, and the yield fell 42 basis points. Bond prices respond to expectations, not just announcements, which is why waiting for RBI to act before adjusting duration usually means acting late.

children.text: Our two illustrative funds: a long duration gilt fund with a modified duration of 8.0, and a short duration fund with a modified duration of 2.0. Each year, a fund's return is roughly its portfolio yield minus expenses, plus the price effect of the yield change, exactly the calculation you did in Chapter 3 and refined in Chapter 4.

body.title: Modelled Annual Returns: Long Duration Gilt vs Short Duration (%)

children.text: The long fund's story is one of extremes: nearly 14% in 2019, almost 12% in 2020, then two years in which it earned essentially nothing, then back to double digits. The short fund never had a spectacular year and never had a bad one. Both were invested in the same market, facing the same RBI.

Short fund: best to worst year

children.text: Over the full cycle the long fund won, by about 1.1 percentage points a year, or roughly ₹92,000 on ₹10 lakh. That is the reward for carrying four times the duration. But the reward was not delivered smoothly, and almost nobody holds an investment through a cycle without reacting to what happens in the middle of it.

body.label: The two years that test every long-duration investor
body.context: Long duration gilt fund against short duration, over two calendar years. Eight percentage points behind, with inflation running above both.

body.title: Estimate a year's fund return
body.prompt: A gilt fund has a portfolio YTM of 7.20%, an expense ratio of 0.40% and a modified duration of 6.5. Over the next year, yields rise by 60 basis points. Ignoring convexity, estimate the fund's total return for the year, as a percentage to two decimal places.
body.explanation: Income = 7.20% − 0.40% = 6.80%. Price effect = −6.5 × 0.0060 × 100 = −3.90%. Total ≈ 6.80% − 3.90% = 2.90%. The income cushion absorbed the loss; a 105 basis point rise would have been needed to wipe it out entirely.

children.text: In 2022 the long fund lost 6.69% on price but still ended only 0.54% down, because a year of coupon income covered most of it. The breakeven idea from Chapter 3 is exactly this: yield divided by duration tells you how big a rise the income can absorb.
The best time to own duration is when yields are high and about to fall.
That was early 2019, when the 10-year yielded 7.37%, and again in early 2023 at 7.33%. The worst time was early 2021, when the yield was 5.90% and had little room to fall but plenty to rise.
Past returns point the wrong way.

After 2019 and 2020, long gilt funds showed the best three-year track records in the category, precisely when the yields that produced those returns had fallen to their lowest. High trailing returns in a bond fund usually mean the gains have already been taken.

body.title: Reading a bond fund's track record
body.question: In January 2021, a long duration gilt fund advertised a three-year return of about 11% a year, well ahead of every short duration fund. The 10-year G-Sec yield was then 5.90%. What did that track record mostly tell an investor?
options: That the fund manager was skilled and would likely repeat it
That yields had already fallen a long way, so the price gains were behind it and its future income was low
That gilt funds are always better than short duration funds
Nothing useful; past returns are random
body.explanation: A bond fund's past return is the yield it started with plus price gains from falling yields. By January 2021 both were exhausted: the starting yield was only 5.90% and yields had little room to fall further. The strong record was a description of what had happened, not a forecast. The next two years returned under 1% in total in our model.

body.title: Long Duration vs Short Duration Through a Full Cycle

columns.label: Long duration gilt fund
points: Higher return over the full six years: 7.35% a year in our model
Return driven by price swings as much as income
Two consecutive years of near-zero returns in the middle
Needs a holding period long enough to survive a hiking cycle
Best bought when yields are high, which usually feels like the worst time

columns.label: Short duration fund
points: Lower return over the full six years: 6.25% a year in our model
No year below 3.96%, so no test of patience
Suits money needed within a few years
Reinvests into higher yields quickly when rates rise

body.title: What cushions a rate rise
body.textWithBlank: When yields rise, a bond fund's ___ income partly offsets the fall in prices, which is why the long gilt fund lost only 0.54% in 2022 despite a 6.69% price fall.
body.explanation: A fund earns its portfolio yield every year regardless of price movements. Yield divided by modified duration gives the rise in yields that would exactly cancel one year of income.

body.title: How these modelled returns were built

children.text: So you can judge the numbers rather than take them on trust, here are the assumptions. Each fund's income for a year is its starting portfolio yield minus its expense ratio, taken as 0.30% for the gilt fund and 0.35% for the short duration fund. The gilt fund's portfolio yield is set equal to the starting 10-year G-Sec yield; the short duration fund's is set 40 basis points lower, reflecting a normal upward-sloping curve. The price effect uses the two-term formula with a modified duration of 8.0 and convexity of 90 for the gilt fund, and 2.0 and 6 for the short duration fund. Duration is held constant all year, and the whole curve is assumed to move by the change in the 10-year yield.

Real funds differ in every one of these respects. Managers change duration through the year, hold state development loans and corporate bonds at higher yields, and earn or lose from curve shape as well as level. Treat the table as a clean experiment in what duration does to a rate cycle, and compare it with published scheme returns on AMFI or an AMC factsheet before drawing conclusions about any real fund.

body.title: Manish chases the 2020 returns
body.scenario: Manish Gupta, a 44-year-old dentist in Indore, checked debt fund returns in January 2021. Long duration gilt funds had delivered around 11% to 12% a year for three years, far ahead of his short duration fund. The 10-year G-Sec yielded 5.90%, the repo rate was 4.00%, and commentators were debating when RBI would start raising rates. He moved ₹15 lakh from his short duration fund into a long duration gilt fund with a modified duration of 8.0.
body.prompt: Using the modelled returns in this lesson, work out what Manish earned over 2021 and 2022 and what he would have earned had he stayed put. Explain the mistake in his reasoning, and what he should have checked before switching.
body.modelAnswer:
1. Long duration gilt fund: 2021 +1.34%, 2022 −0.54%. Two-year total about +0.79%, so ₹15 lakh became roughly ₹15.12 lakh.
2. Short duration fund, had he stayed: 2021 +4.06%, 2022 +3.96%. Two-year total about +9.01%, so ₹15 lakh would have been roughly ₹16.35 lakh. The switch cost him about ₹1.23 lakh over two years, before tax and exit loads.
3. The mistake: he treated a bond fund's past return as a forecast. Those 11% to 12% returns came from yields falling from 7.37% to 5.90%. Once that had happened, the fund offered a 5.90% starting yield and eight years of duration pointing at a rate cycle that could only realistically turn upward.
4. What he should have checked: (a) the starting portfolio YTM, which caps what the fund can earn without price gains; (b) modified duration against his own horizon; (c) the breakeven, 5.90 ÷ 8.0 ≈ 0.74, meaning a rise of just 74 basis points would wipe out a year's income, and the market moved 55 and 88 basis points in the next two years; (d) whether he needed the money within a few years, in which case duration 8.0 was never appropriate.
5. What he did right, eventually: he held on. From 2023 the long fund returned 8.24% and 10.32% in our model, as the higher yields he had bought into finally paid. Investors who switched back after 2022 would have missed that.
6. The general rule: choose duration by matching it to your horizon and the yield on offer today, never by ranking last three years' returns.

points: Between 2019 and 2024 India ran a full cycle: repo from 6.50% down to 4.00%, back up to 6.50%, with the 10-year yield swinging roughly 150 basis points either way.
In our model, the long duration gilt fund returned 7.35% a year over six years against 6.25% for a short duration fund, but with a far bumpier path.
The long fund's yearly returns ranged from +13.93% to −0.54%; the short fund's from +8.28% to +3.96%.
Across 2021 and 2022 together, the long fund returned about 0.79% against 9.01% for the short fund.
Income is the shock absorber: a 6.69% price fall in 2022 became a 0.54% loss once a year of yield was counted.
Yields move on expectations, not just RBI announcements: the 10-year moved 55 and 42 basis points in years when the repo rate never changed.
A bond fund's strong trailing return usually means its yields have already fallen, so the easy gains are behind it.

body.text: This lesson is for education only and is not investment advice. Fund returns shown are modelled from approximate yield levels using simplified assumptions, and are not the returns of any actual scheme; 10-year G-Sec yield levels are rounded approximations. Repo rate decisions are as announced by RBI. Past rate cycles do not predict future ones. Mutual fund investments are subject to market risks; read all scheme-related documents carefully and consult a SEBI-registered investment adviser before investing.
